STATE OF ARKANSAS

THE ATTORNEY GENERAL
Dustin McDANIEL

Opinion No. 2012-001

January 12, 2012

Mr. Jeff C. Harper, City Attorney
City of Springdale

201 North Spring Street

Post Office Box 1208

Springdale, Arkansas 72765

Dear Mr. Harper:

You have requested my opinion regarding the Arkansas Freedom of Information
Act (“FOIA”). The basis for your request is A.C.A. § 25-19-105(c)(3)(B)(@) (Supp.
2011), which authorizes the custodian, requester, or the subject of personnel or
employee evaluation records to seek an opinion from this office stating whether
the custodian’s decision concerning the release of such records is consistent with
the FOIA.

You report that the City’s records custodian received a FOIA request on January 5,
2012, for “any emails found on [former fire chief] Everett Duane Atha’s work-
issued Dell desktop computer, from July 1, 2011 through December 31, 2011, as
well as any and all pictures or .jpeg files stored on the computer....”” You state
that after reviewing the emails, it was determined they fall into two categories,
which you describe as “emails directly related to work and personal emails.” You
state that the photos were similarly categorized as “photos of a personal nature and
photos that were job related.”

You have advised the custodian that all of the emails and photos constitute
“personnel records” that are subject to release under the FOIA, after shielding the
identities of non-employees from certain photos. The former fire chief’s attorney
has objected to the release of what you have called the “personal emails” and the
“personal photos.” It is his position that these items are not “public records” under

' You report that Mr. Atha retired from the City of Springdale on December 28, 2011.

TELEPHONE (501) 682-2007 * Fax (501) 682-8084
INTERNET WEBSITE * http://www.ag.state.ar.us/
 Jeff C. Harper, Springdale City Att’y
Opinion No. 2012-001
Page 2

the FOIA. He also objects to what both you and he refer to as the “job related
photos” to the extent that any such photos may have been the subject of an internal
investigation. Another attorney for one of the individuals depicted in the so-called
‘job related photos” contends that these photos do not fall within the FOIA’s
definition of “public records.”

You have submitted for my review both the “job related photos” (labeled “Exhibit
A”), and samples of the “personal emails” (“Exhibit C”) and “personal photos”
(“Exhibit B’”). I will refer to the records by their corresponding “Exhibit”
designation.

RESPONSE

My duty under A.C.A. § 25-19-105(c)(3)(B)(i) is to determine whether the
custodian’s decision as to the release of personnel or evaluation records is
consistent with the FOIA. As I have previously noted, my statutory mandate
under A.C.A. § 25-19-105(c)(3)(A) and (B) is premised upon the assumption that
the records in question are “public records.”” It appears that in this instance, the
primary or initial issue is not whether the records are exempt from disclosure, but
instead whether the records come within the threshold requirement of being
“public records” under the FOIA. This issue is not within my statutory power of
review under A.C.A. § 25-19-105(c)(3)(B).°

* See Op. Att’y Gen. 2008-095 (noting that these subsections presume that the records are “personnel or
evaluation records,” and thus necessarily “public records,” and that the Attorney General’s duty appears
restricted to opining on whether the custodian’s decision as to the exemption of records is consistent with
the FOIA.)

The FOIA defines “public records” as follows:

“Public records” means writings, recorded sounds, films, tapes, electronic or computer-
based information, or data compilations in any medium required by law to be kept or
otherwise kept and that constitute a record of the performance or lack of performance of
official functions that are or should be carried out by a public official or employee, a
governmental agency, or any other agency or improvement district that is wholly or
partially supported by public funds or expending public funds. All records maintained in
public offices or by public employees within the scope of their employment shall be
presumed to be public records.

A.C.A. § 25-19-103(5)(A) (Supp. 2011).

3 Op. 2008-095, supra. As I noted in the latter opinion, records held by a public entity are rebuttably
presumed to be “public records” under the FOIA:
 Jeff C. Harper, Springdale City Att’y
Opinion No. 2012-001
Page 3

Because I can only opine regarding the possible exemption of the emails and
photos, I must assume for purposes of this opinion that each of the records you
have provided in fact meets the definition of a “public record." With that
assumption in mind, it is my opinion that with a few exceptions concerning
Exhibit C, you have properly decided that the records are subject to disclosure
under the test for “personnel records.”” As explained below, Exhibit C appears to
contain some financial information that must be redacted. I must emphasize,
however, that my conclusion regarding the records’ release is premised upon the
assumption that the Exhibits are “public records” as defined by the FOIA.

DISCUSSION

You have determined that the relevant exemption is the one for “personnel
records.” The FOIA exempts from disclosure “personnel records to the extent that
disclosure would constitute a clearly unwarranted invasion of personal privacy.”
The FOIA does not define the phrase “clearly unwarranted invasion of personal
privacy.” The Arkansas Supreme Court has construed the phrase, however, and
has applied a balancing test that requires weighing the interest of the public in
accessing the records against the individual’s interest in keeping the records
private.’ If the public’s interest outweighs the individual’s interest, the release of

There is a presumption that all records kept in public offices by public employees within
the scope of their employment are “public records.” The presumption may be rebutted,
however, with evidence that the records do not “reflect the performance or lack of
performance of official functions.” A.C.A. § 25-19-103(5)(A). This is a fact question
that can only be answered after a review of the actual content of the [records] in question
and after consideration of any other pertinent facts. This issue was discussed at length in
Pulaski County v. Arkansas Democrat Gazette Inc., 370 Ark. 435, [260 S.W.3d 718]
(2007) and Pulaski County v. Arkansas Democrat-Gazette, Inc., 371 Ark. 217, [264
S.W.3d 46] (2007).

Id. at 6-7.

‘ The FOIA plainly does not require disclosure of records not falling with the act’s definition of “public
records.” I am neither authorized nor equipped, however, to assess whether the presumption of “public
record” status noted above is actually rebutted with respect to the emails and photos at issue in the case at
hand. I lack sufficient facts to make that threshold determination; and as indicated above, the question in
any event is outside my statutory mandate. I must instead refer you, the custodian, and any other interested
parties in this regard to the decisions in Pulaski County, supra, note 3.

> This also assumes, as explained further below, that each of the records constitutes a personnel record. As
explained further below, it may be a question of fact whether each of the records is a personnel record.

§ A.C.A. § 25-19-105(b)(12) (Supp. 2011).

7 Young v. Rice, 308 Ark. 593, 826 S.W.2d 252 (1992).
 Jeff C. Harper, Springdale City Att’y
Opinion No. 2012-001
Page 4

the records will not constitute a “clearly unwarranted invasion of personal
privacy.” The balancing takes place with a thumb on the scale favoring
disclosure. The court in Young noted the following regarding the test:

The fact that section 25-19-105(b)(10) [now subsection 105(b)(12)]
exempts disclosure of personnel records only when a clearly
unwarranted personal privacy invasion would result, indicates that
certain ‘warranted’ privacy invasions will be tolerated. Thus, section
25-19-105(b)(10) requires that the public’s right to knowledge of the
records be weighed against an _ individual’s right to
privacy....Because section 25-19-105(b)(10) allows warranted
invasions of privacy, it follows that when the public’s interest is
substantial, it will usually outweigh any individual privacy interests
and disclosure will be favored.*

If there is little public interest in information, however, the privacy interest will
prevail if it is not insubstantial.’ Additionally, given that exemptions from
disclosure must be narrowly construed,” it is the burden of an individual resisting
disclosure to establish that his “privacy interests outweighed that of the public’s
under the circumstances presented,”

Turning to the records in question, it is my opinion that you have in all likelihood
properly identified the “personnel records” exemption as the relevant exemption to
consider when addressing Exhibits A, B, and C. The other potentially applicable
exemption is the one for “employee evaluation or job performance records,”

which the FOIA likewise does not define. This office has consistently opined,
however, that the phrase refers to records that were created by (or at the behest of)

* 308 Ark. at 598.

° Stilley v. McBride, 332 Ark. 306, 965 S.W.2d 125 (1998).
10 & g., Orsini v. State, 340 Ark. 665, 13 S.W.3d 167 (2000).
i Stilley, supra, 332 Ark. at 313.

2 ACA. § 25-19-105(c)(1) (Supp. 2011). “Employee evaluation or job performance records” are
releasable only if the following three conditions have been met: (1). There has been a final administrative
resolution of any suspension or termination proceeding; (2) The records in question formed a basis for the
decision made in that proceeding to suspend or terminate the employee; and (3) There is a compelling
public interest in the disclosure of the records in question. Employee evaluation or job performance
records cannot be released unless each prong of this test has been met.
 Jeff C. Harper, Springdale City Att’y
Opinion No. 2012-001
Page 5

the employer and that detail the employce’s performance or lack of performance
on the job.’ This exception includes records generated while investigating
allegations of employee misconduct that detail incidents that gave rise to an
allegation of misconduct.'* But as stated by one of my predecessors,
“Tdjocuments not created in the evaluation process do not come within the
rationale behind the 25-19-105(c)(1) exemption.””” Accordingly, pre-existing,
otherwise public records that have been included in an internal affairs file, but
which were not generated as a result of the investigation, ordinarily do not
constitute employee evaluation or job performance records.'° As stated by one of
my predecessors, “[t]he fact that a previously created record is later used in an
internal investigation of an employee does not transform the record into an
employee evaluation/job performance record.”’’ I have explained the basis for this
differentiation as follows:

At least one rationale for focusing on the circumstances surrounding
the creation of records, as opposed to their later use, arises from the
reasons underlying the exemption.... [T]he exemption for employee
evaluation or job performance records:

reflects the public interest in maintaining an
effective public employee evaluation system as well as
the privacy interests of employees. Without an
exemption for such records, supervisory personnel
who perform the evaluations may not be candid in
assessing employee performance. Also, routine
disclosure of the records could undermine one
important objective of the evaluation process-
identification of weaknesses with an eye toward
fostering improvement — by revealing an employee’s

'3 E g., Op Att’y Gen. 2011-100 (and opinions cited therein).

* Id.

'S Op. Att’y Gen. 2005-267 (quoting Op. Att’y Gen. 2005-094). See also Op. Att’y Gen. 2001-142
(“Records generated by third parties, and not at the behest of someone in a position to evaluate the
employee, generally do not constitute job performance or evaluation records.”).

'© Op. Att’y Gen. 2008-172.

” Op. Att’y Gen. 2005-032.
 Jeff C. Harper, Springdale City Att’y
Opinion No. 2012-001
Page 6

deficiencies before he has an opportunity to correct
them.

It is difficult to conclude that the listed purposes of the exemption
are fostered where the record was not initially created in the
evaluation process, but was only later used for that purpose. For
example, disclosure of records not created for the purposes of
evaluating an employee would presumably not affect the candor of
an evaluator. This consideration is reinforced by the principle that
exemptions from disclosure in the FOIA are to be construed
narrowly.'®

Viewing Exhibits A, B, and C in light of the foregoing, I believe it is clear that
none of the records constitutes an “employee evaluation or job performance
record.” It has been suggested that all or parts of Exhibit A may fall within that
exemption, but there is no indication that any of these records were created by or
at the behest of the employer for evaluation purposes.

29

Turning, then, to the categorization of the records as “personnel records,” it is
difficult to determine from the face of the records whether in fact each falls within
this exemption. The FOIA does not define the term “personnel records,” nor are
there any helpful Arkansas cases construing the term or stating whether “personal”
records such as Exhibit B (the “personal photos”) or Exhibit C (“personal emails”’)
are properly classified as “personnel records” for purposes of A.C.A. § 25-19-
105(b)(12). When addressing this exemption, my predecessors and I have given
the term “personnel records” a broad interpretation, stating that it encompasses
any records (other than evaluation or job performance records) that pertain to or
relate to the individual employee.” I nevertheless cannot definitively determine
whether Exhibits B and C sufficiently relate to an individual employee or
employees, such that they are properly classified as “personnel records.” This is
likely a question of fact that depends upon the specific circumstances surrounding
their creation.

'8 Op. Att’y Gen. 2007-313, at n. 3 (internal citations omitted).

° Eg, Op. Atty Gen. 2010-099; see Op. Att’y Gen. 2010-006 (and opinions cited therein). Two
recognized commentators on the FOIA have further observed that “documents that only tangentially relate
to an employee” are not covered by the exemption. John J. Watkins & Richard J. Peltz, THE ARKANSAS
FREEDOM OF INFORMATION ACT, 188-89 (Arkansas Law Press, 5th ed., 2009) (citing Op. Att’y Gen.
Nos. 2007-255 and 94-391). I have also suggested that the exemption probably does not cover records that
do not relate to any matter involving an individual employee’s status as an employee. Op. Att’y Gen.
2008-095.
 Jeff C. Harper, Springdale City Atty
Opinion No. 2012-001
Page 7

Assuming, however, that you are correct in determining that they constitute
personnel records, then in my opinion the balancing test described above likely
weighs in favor of releasing Exhibits B and C, with a few exceptions.” Exhibit C
(the emails) includes two communications that pertain to financial transactions. In
my opinion, the test weighs in favor of the nondisclosure of the financial
information contained in these records, including the names of the institutions. As
for the remaining records, according to my review, none of them contains
information the release of which would constitute a clearly unwarranted invasion
of the employee’s personal privacy.”

As for Exhibit A, again assuming these records meet the FOJA’s definition of
“public records,” then in my opinion the records that depict public employees
likely constitute “personnel records.”** Although you have provided no
information in support of your conclusion that the balancing test weighs in favor
of disclosing these records, I believe it can be determined from a review of the
records themselves that the public’s significant interest in the ones depicting
public employees outweighs the employees’ interest in shielding their identities.

With regard to the remainder of Exhibit A, I cannot determine based merely upon
a review of these records whether they sufficiently relate to an individual
employee or employees, such that they are properly classified as “personnel
records.” As with Exhibits B and C, if these records are not personnel records, I
have no authority to review the custodian’s decision. It may well be, on the other
hand, that the surrounding circumstances justify their classification as personnel
records. But this presents a question of fact that J am unable to resolve based upon
the face of the records only.

If a factual review nevertheless establishes that the remainder of Exhibit A
constitutes personnel records, then in my opinion your decision to release the
records after shielding the non-employees’ identities is consistent with the FOIA.
I believe the non-employees’ constitutional privacy interest likely supports

2° must reiterate that this discussion assumes the records in fact constitute “public records.”

21 Tf Exhibits B and C are not properly considered personnel records, then I have no authority to review the
custodian’s decision in the first place. But I will nevertheless note that assuming they are “public records,”
these Exhibits would have to be released because the records would be mere public records not subject to
any exemption.

*2 See Op. Att’y Gen. 2007-213 (opining that a photograph of a city police department employee that was
maintained by the department related to the individual’s employment and was a personnel record).
 Jeff C. Harper, Springdale City Att’y
Opinion No. 2012-001
Page 8

shielding their identities, whether these records are released as personnel records
or as mere public records.”

Deputy Attorney General Elisabeth A. Walker prepared the foregoing opinion,
which I hereby approve.

Sincerely,

DUSTIN MCDANIEL
Attorney General

specific disclosure requirements of the FOIA, at least with regard to the release of documents containing
constitutionally protectable information. McCambridge v. City of Little Rock, 298 Ark. 219, 766 S.W.2d
909 (1989). For a discussion of this issue, see generally Op. Att’y Gen. 2003-015.
